Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: The equation used to convert the measured quantities into an age or date, together with a citation for that equation.
Name the equation unambiguously; where a procedure supports more than one, state which is used and under what conditions.

Reason: external reporting standards require it — provenance, not our Column C (W3)
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Required by every geochronology reporting standard surveyed (Condon et al. 2024; Schaen et al. 2021; Rooney et al. 2024; Flowers et al. 2024; Kohn et al. 2024; Mahan et al. 2023).
Distinct from Age Model and Software, which records how multiple analyses are combined into a single reported result.
The kind of date or age the procedure reports.

Reason: why a bare age is ambiguous
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Most dating systems derive several different date types from the same measurements, so a reported age is ambiguous without this.
Where more than one type is reported, list all, separated by semicolons.

Reason: external standard provenance (W3)
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Kohn et al. (2024) carry this as a named required item ("fission-track age type"); the equivalent distinction is required by all five other standards surveyed.
How any non-radiogenic, inherited or pre-existing component of the measured signal was accounted for, including the composition assumed, its source, and its uncertainty.
Record 'None' where the measured quantity accumulates from zero and no such component exists.

Reason: scope rationale — which dating systems it applies to
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Applies to five of the six dating systems surveyed; fission track is the sole genuine exception, as tracks accumulate from zero.

Reason: the sentence exists to justify the D tier; that is what Column D encodes
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: D=Editable rather than Read-Only: the procedure registers the correction method and any default composition, but the value actually applied is frequently sample-specific (a two-stage model composition is evaluated at the interpreted age) or session-derived (a trapped composition solved from an isochron intercept), and a revision to the assumed composition should not require registering a new procedure.

Reason: library-internal design cross-reference to Rule 5
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Same reasoning as Rule 5's Constants and Reference Values Used.
The proportion of the measured signal that is radiogenic, as opposed to inherited, initial or otherwise non-radiogenic.

Reason: 'records what the session actually produced' restates C=N/A; the companion boundary is real
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Measured companion to Inherited or Initial Signal Correction, which is procedure-level: this field records what the session actually produced.

Reason: why the fraction matters for interpreting the age
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: It indicates how strongly the reported age depends on the assumed non-radiogenic composition — a result derived from a low radiogenic fraction is sensitive to that assumption in a way a high-fraction result is not, and that sensitivity is invisible from the age and its uncertainty alone.

Reason: library-internal design note — criterion-versus-measurement split
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Follows the criterion-versus-measurement split used for Oxide Production.
The statistical model used to combine individual analyses into a single reported age, including any criteria governing which model is applied.

Reason: why the model choice changes the result
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: This is a methodological choice that changes the result: a Model-1 and a Model-3 regression of the same data yield different ages and different uncertainties.

Record the model only — the software implementing it belongs in Data Reduction Software (Group 3), whose scope already extends to age calculation; where reduction and age regression use different packages, list both there.

Reason: external standard provenance (W3)
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Required in some form by all six geochronology reporting standards surveyed.
The zero point from which the reported age is measured, where this is not the present day, and the date it corresponds to.
Record 'Present day' where the conventional datum applies.

Reason: external requirement plus concrete per-system instructions
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Explicitly required wherever the datum is not the present: year of sample collection for luminescence (Mahan et al. 2023), end of irradiation for 40Ar/39Ar decay corrections (Schaen et al. 2021).

The rules determining which individual analyses contribute to a reported aggregate result, together with the outcome of applying them: how many analyses were acquired, how many were included, and on what grounds any were excluded.
Distinct from within-analysis outlier filtering, which removes anomalous points inside a single analysis: this field decides which whole analyses enter the reported value.

Reason: design rationale for combining criteria and outcome
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Criteria and outcome are combined in one field because neither is interpretable without the other, following the precision/accuracy precedent.
The statistic reported to show whether scatter among the contributing analyses exceeds what analytical uncertainty alone predicts, together with its value.

Reason: what the statistic answers
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Answers whether a reported aggregate is defensible as a single population.

Reason: explains C=N/A explicitly, then adds a real boundary about the threshold
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Procedure-level tier is N/A because the value cannot be known before the analysis; the procedure may still state an acceptance threshold, which belongs with the inclusion criteria.
The rules governing which part of the sample is analysed, and why.
Covers the criteria applied when choosing grains, aliquots, spots, or a region of interest — size, morphology, clarity, freedom from inclusions or alteration, phase identity, or spatial position.
Distinct from Target Material, which states the material type the procedure is designed for: this field states how, within such a sample, the analysed portion is picked out.

Distinct from any imaging the procedure performs as its own measurement.
Where the imaging is performed on a separate instrument, it should also be recorded in the Group 1 coupling fields.

The chemical species this procedure is designed to determine, recorded at whatever resolution the chemistry is resolved — element(s) for this technique; valence species where a procedure resolves oxidation state; compounds where it resolves molecules.
Isotopes are not analytes: isotopes of an element are the same chemical species.

Reason: 'procedure registers the suite; at analysis level the analyst records the subset' is the C/D split
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: The procedure registers the full analyte suite; at analysis level the analyst records the specific subset actually measured in the session, which may be narrower if species were excluded due to interferences or scope reduction.

Reason: restates what Column I encodes
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Fields whose Keyed By column declares 'analyte' apply individually to each entry in this list.

Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Companion to the blank correction method, which is procedure-level: this field records what was actually measured.

Reason: library-internal design note
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Follows the criterion-versus-measurement split the library applies wherever a procedure sets a threshold and an analysis reports a value against it.
An externally-calibrated factor that converts the measured quantity into the reported quantity, how it was determined, and its uncertainty.
Applies where the conversion depends on a factor calibrated against a reference of independently known value, rather than on the instrument response alone.
Distinct from the fields that name the calibration material and that state which approach applies to which analyte, where the technique has them: this field records the resulting factor itself.
Description of the multi-collector Faraday cup array.

Specify the total number of Faraday cup detectors (fixed and moveable), their labeled positions (e.g., L4, L3, L2, L1, Ax, H1, H2, H3, H4 for a 9-cup Neptune), and the presence and position of any ion counter (SEM) or Daly detector in the collector block.

Reason: why cup count and span matter
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: The number and span of cups constrains which isotope combinations can be simultaneously collected.
Resistance values (Ω) of the feedback resistors in the Faraday cup amplifiers.
Standard amplifiers use 10¹¹ Ω resistors, yielding 1 V per ~6.24 × 10⁶ ion counts per second.

Reason: why high-gain amplifiers are fitted
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: High-gain amplifiers (10¹² or 10¹³ Ω) are fitted to selected cups to improve signal-to-noise for very low-intensity beams (e.g., 234U, low-abundance spike isotopes).
Report the resistor value per cup position, or note 'all 10¹¹ Ω' if uniform.
Method used to calibrate the relative gain (amplification factor) of each Faraday cup amplifier at the start of or during each analytical session.

Reason: why gain differences must be corrected
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Relative gain differences between amplifiers cause systematic errors in isotope ratios if uncorrected.

Common approaches: instrument internal gain calibration routine (measures signal in each cup sequentially using a common beam), amplifier rotation procedure, or measurement of a known isotope ratio solution in each cup.
For instruments with SEM detectors, also describes the SEM-to-Faraday cross-calibration sequence.
Specify frequency (per session, per block, weekly).
Assignment of isotope masses to Faraday cup or ion counter detector positions for this procedure, and the analyte each position serves.
Lists the mass number monitored in each collector position with its analyte element where it has one — e.g. 'L3=116Sn (Sn); L2=117Sn (Sn); Ax=120Sn (Sn); H1=121Sb (interference monitor, no analyte)'.

Interference-monitor and internal-standard positions serve no analyte and carry no parent element; the analyte list itself is given by the Analyte field and is never inferred from the mass labels here.
For static multi-collection procedures, one configuration applies throughout the measurement.
For multi-dynamic procedures, list all configurations and the cycling sequence.

Reason: why assignments differ between element systems
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Different element systems require different mass assignments within the collector array span.
Number of measurement blocks acquired per sample or standard solution introduction.
In MC-ICP-MS, data are structured as blocks of cycles; each block typically begins with a baseline (on-peak zero) measurement before the analytical cycles.

Reason: why multiple blocks are useful
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Multiple blocks per sample allow inspection of signal stability and within-measurement drift.

Reason: 'procedure specifies; analyst may adjust' is the D=Editable definition
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Procedure specifies the standard number; analyst may adjust for samples with low signal or for high-precision requirements.
Number of measurement cycles acquired per block.
One cycle corresponds to a single set of simultaneous Faraday cup readings integrated for the duration specified in Integration Time per Cycle.
Total integration time per sample = (Number of Cycles per Block) × (Integration Time per Cycle) × (Number of Blocks per Measurement).

Reason: as above
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Procedure specifies the standard value; analyst may adjust within procedure bounds.
Duration of signal integration per measurement cycle (seconds).

Reason: what it determines
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Determines counting statistics per cycle.

Reason: the precision/drift trade-off
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Longer integration times improve shot-noise precision but increase the impact of signal drift within the integration window.

Reason: why high-gain channels need longer integration
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: For high-gain (10¹² or 10¹³ Ω) amplifier channels, longer integration times are often required to accumulate sufficient charge.

Reason: as above
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Procedure specifies the standard integration time; analyst may confirm or adjust within procedure bounds.
Where different isotope channels use different integration schemes, record the time for each channel.
Method and timing for measuring the ion beam baseline (on-peak zero) during acquisition, and the portion of the acquisition it is taken from.

Reason: enumerates the three approaches (definition) with the reason each applies (rationale)
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Three approaches are in use and the choice depends on how sample reaches the plasma: deflecting the ion beam (beam-off or electrostatic deflector); aspirating an acid blank, which applies only to solution introduction; or, for laser ablation, collecting a defined number of laser-off cycles at the start of the same block, since no blank can be aspirated mid-ablation.
State which, and how many cycles or how long.
Mathematical law used to parameterize instrumental isotope mass fractionation as a function of mass difference.

Reason: why the exponential law is preferred
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: The exponential law (Maréchal et al. 1999) is most widely used and theoretically best justified for MC-ICP-MS.
The linear law assumes fractionation proportional to mass difference.
The power law is an alternative formulation.
For double-spike procedures, the law is embedded in the inversion algorithm and must be consistent between spike calibration and sample data reduction.

Field: Internal Normalization Element and Isotope Ratio
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Element and isotope ratio used as the internal normalization standard for mass bias correction.

Field: Internal Normalization Element and Isotope Ratio
Reason: mechanism — how the correction works
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: The measured ratio of the normalizing element is used to calculate the mass bias factor β using the chosen mass fractionation law, which is then applied to correct the analyte isotope ratios assuming β_norm ≈ β_analyte.

Field: Internal Normalization Element and Isotope Ratio
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Specify the element, the monitored isotope ratio (e.g., 113Cd/111Cd for Sb measurements), and the certified or consensus value used for correction.

Field: Internal Normalization Element and Isotope Ratio
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Record 'N/A' if internal normalization is not used.

The pair of enriched isotopes used to construct the double spike.

Reason: selection constraints plus the reason for them
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Both isotopes must be naturally rare, free from isobaric interferences, and chosen to minimize error magnification in the inversion.
The double spike composition must be accurately calibrated before use.
Specify both isotope masses and the spike certificate or calibration reference.
Record 'N/A' if double-spike method is not used.

Reason: why an optimum exists plus how it is determined
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: An optimal mixing ratio minimizes error propagation through the double-spike inversion; the optimum is analyte-system specific and is typically determined using the Double Spike Toolbox or equivalent.
The achieved mixing ratio may deviate from the target within acceptable bounds (typically ±20% of optimal); the double-spike inversion corrects for actual mixing ratios.
Record 'N/A' if double-spike method is not used.

Common implementations: iterative Newton-Raphson solution, matrix algebraic approach, or published software (e.g., Rudge et al. 2009 Double Spike Toolbox).
Specify the algorithm or software reference and version.
Record 'N/A' if double-spike method is not used.

Method used to verify that every collector sits on a flat region of its peak top simultaneously, and the acceptance threshold applied before analysis begins.

Reason: why simultaneous collection makes peak flatness critical
Sentence_TEXT_UNCHANGED: Specific to simultaneous collection: a sequential instrument centres one mass at a time, whereas a multi-collector array must have all cups on flat peak tops at once or the measured ratio carries a peak-shape bias that no downstream correction removes.
Typically assessed by scanning across the peak plateau, or by comparing ratios measured at slightly offset mass positions.
